title: HTML from Scratch: Tags, Elements & Semantic Pages
plainExplanation:
HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the skeleton of every webpage on the internet. Just like a newspaper has a headline, subheadings, paragraphs, and images, HTML uses simple angle-bracket tags like

and

to tell the web browser what each piece of content means.
whyItMatters: Before you can style a website with CSS or make it interactive with JavaScript, you need clean, accessible HTML structure. Search engines, screen readers, and browsers rely on semantic HTML to understand your page.
learningObjectives: Understand what an HTML element, opening tag, closing tag, and attribute are
Build a complete webpage using semantic landmarks (<header>, <main>, <article>, <footer>)
Create accessible links, images with alt text, lists, and forms
commonMistakes: Using <div> for everything instead of meaningful tags like <button>, <nav>, and <main>
Forgetting the alt attribute on images, which breaks accessibility for screen readers

questions.prompt: Why should you use a <button> tag instead of a clickable <div> for actions on a webpage?
options: <div> tags cannot have click events in browsers
<button> gives built-in keyboard navigation, focus handling, and screen-reader semantics
<button> makes the website download faster
HTML forbids using <div> inside <main>
questions.correctAnswer: <button> gives built-in keyboard navigation, focus handling, and screen-reader semantics
questions.explanation: Native <button> elements automatically support Enter/Space activation, Tab focus, and announce themselves as buttons to assistive technologies.

questions.prompt: Which HTML tag represents the primary, unique content area of a page?
options: <top>
<main>
<center>
<body-content>
questions.explanation: <main> is a standard semantic landmark that tells browsers and screen readers where the core page content begins.

questions.prompt: Spot the accessibility issue in this image tag:
options: Images must end with </img>
It is missing a descriptive alt attribute
src must be uppercase SRC
PNG files cannot be used in HTML
questions.correctAnswer: It is missing a descriptive alt attribute
questions.explanation: The alt attribute provides text if the image fails to load and lets visually impaired learners understand what the image shows.

title: CSS Layout Mastery: Box Model, Flexbox & Responsive Grid
plainExplanation: If HTML is the skeleton of a house, CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the paint, furniture placement, and room dimensions. Every element on a webpage is a rectangular box made of content, padding (space inside), border (the frame), and margin (space outside).
whyItMatters: Users view websites on phones, tablets, and wide desktop monitors. Mastering the Box Model, Flexbox (1D rows/columns), and CSS Grid (2D layouts) lets you build clean, responsive interfaces that never break or overlap.
learningObjectives: Explain the CSS Box Model: content, padding, border, and margin
Align items in rows and columns with Flexbox (justify-content, align-items, gap)
Create responsive multi-column layouts using CSS Grid and media queries
commonMistakes: Confusing padding (space inside the border) with margin (space outside the border)
Setting fixed pixel widths like width: 900px that cause horizontal scrolling on phones

assessment.title: CSS Box Model & Responsive Layout Check

questions.prompt: Which property adds breathing room INSIDE a button between its text and its border?
options: margin
padding
z-index
float
questions.explanation: Padding sits inside the border around the content, whereas margin pushes neighboring elements away outside the border.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer CSS Grid over Flexbox?
options: When you need to control both rows and columns simultaneously in a 2D layout
Only when changing text colors
Only on mobile screens
CSS Grid replaces HTML completely
questions.correctAnswer: When you need to control both rows and columns simultaneously in a 2D layout
questions.explanation: Flexbox excels at one-dimensional alignment (a row or a column), while CSS Grid excels at two-dimensional layouts (rows AND columns together).

codingChallenge.title: Calculate Total Box Width
codingChallenge.instructions: Write a JavaScript function `totalBoxWidth(contentWidth, paddingX, borderX)` that calculates the total rendered width under standard `content-box` sizing: `contentWidth + (paddingX * 2) + (borderX * 2)`.

hiddenTests.description: Handles border of 1px on both sides

codingChallenge.solutionHint: Both left and right sides contribute padding and border, so multiply each by 2 and add to contentWidth.

title: JavaScript Fundamentals, Events & DOM Manipulation
plainExplanation: JavaScript is the brain that makes webpages come alive. It runs right inside your web browser to respond when a user clicks a button, validates a form before submitting, fetches live data from servers, and updates the screen without reloading the page.
whyItMatters: JavaScript is the only programming language built natively into every web browser on earth. Learning it unlocks frontend web development, backend Node.js servers, and cross-platform mobile apps.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with const and let and understand primitive vs object types
Transform arrays cleanly using map, filter, and reduce
Respond to user interactions with event listeners and update the DOM safely
commonMistakes: Using == instead of === which causes surprising type coercion bugs like '5' == 5
Inserting untrusted user input with innerHTML instead of textContent (which creates XSS security bugs)

questions.prompt: Why should you prefer `textContent` over `innerHTML` when displaying text typed by a user?
options: textContent prevents injected HTML/script tags from executing (blocking XSS attacks)
innerHTML does not work in modern browsers
textContent automatically translates text into other languages
innerHTML only works on numbers
questions.correctAnswer: textContent prevents injected HTML/script tags from executing (blocking XSS attacks)
questions.explanation: textContent treats the value strictly as plain text, neutralizing malicious <script> tags.
filter keeps only elements where the callback returns true — here, even numbers whose remainder mod 2 is 0.

codingChallenge.instructions: Write a JavaScript function `getActiveTitles(tasks)` where `tasks` is an array of `{ title: string, done: boolean }`. Return an array of the `title` strings for tasks where `done === false`.

hiddenTests.description: Returns empty array when all tasks are done

title: Component-Driven UI: Props, State & Unidirectional Data Flow
plainExplanation: Imagine building a complex dashboard with LEGO bricks instead of carving it from one giant block of wood. React lets you break your user interface into reusable components (like Navbar, LessonCard, QuizModal). When your data (State) changes, React automatically updates only the exact parts of the screen that depend on it.
whyItMatters: Modern web apps manage hundreds of interactive states simultaneously. Component architecture with TypeScript prevents UI desynchronization bugs and powers most production web applications today.
learningObjectives: Think in components: split UI into clean, single-responsibility building blocks
Pass read-only data down via props and manage interactive changes with state
Update arrays and objects immutably so React detects state changes reliably
commonMistakes: Mutating state arrays directly with state.push(item) instead of creating a new array [...state, item]
Putting derived values into redundant state instead of computing them during render

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid calling `items.push(newItem)` directly on a React state array?
options: JavaScript arrays do not have a push method
Mutating the existing array keeps the same object reference, so React may skip re-rendering
push() deletes the previous elements
React only supports strings in state
questions.correctAnswer: Mutating the existing array keeps the same object reference, so React may skip re-rendering
questions.explanation: React compares state references with Object.is(). Creating a new array `[...items, newItem]` guarantees a new reference and triggers a clean UI update.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between props and state in React?
options: Props are passed into a component from its parent (read-only); state is managed internally by the component
Props can only hold numbers; state can only hold booleans
State is shared across all users on the internet; props are private
There is no difference
questions.correctAnswer: Props are passed into a component from its parent (read-only); state is managed internally by the component
questions.explanation: Props flow downward from parent to child like function arguments, while state represents data that changes over time inside a component.

visibleTests.description: Flips l1 from false to true

moduleTitle: Mobile App Engineering: Touch UX & Cross-Platform Architecture
title: Mobile-First Layouts, Touch Targets & Screen Navigation
plainExplanation: Mobile apps are used with thumbs on small vertical screens while people walk or commute. Unlike desktop websites with mouse cursors and hover states, mobile apps rely on stack navigation (pushing/popping screens), bottom tab bars, large 44px touch targets, and smooth 60fps gestures.
whyItMatters: Over half of global internet traffic happens on smartphones. Understanding mobile navigation stacks, safe areas (notches), and touch ergonomics applies across React Native, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Kotlin Compose.
learningObjectives: Design thumb-friendly layouts with safe area insets and minimum 44x44px touch targets
Model app navigation using Stack, Tab, and Modal navigators
Handle offline-first local storage and network reconnection gracefully
commonMistakes: Placing primary buttons too close to screen notches or bottom home indicator bars
Designing hover-only interactions that do not exist on touchscreens

questions.prompt: How does a Stack Navigator behave when a user taps a list item and then taps Back?
options: It pushes the detail screen onto the top of the stack, and pops it off when going back
It deletes the previous screen from memory permanently
It reloads the entire phone operating system
It opens a desktop browser window
questions.correctAnswer: It pushes the detail screen onto the top of the stack, and pops it off when going back
questions.explanation: Stack navigation follows LIFO (Last-In, First-Out), preserving scroll position and state of previous screens.

questions.prompt: Why is Safe Area padding critical in mobile app layouts?
options: It prevents content and buttons from being hidden under camera notches, status bars, and bottom gesture handles
It encrypts user passwords automatically
It doubles battery life
It converts iOS apps into Android apps
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents content and buttons from being hidden under camera notches, status bars, and bottom gesture handles
questions.explanation: Modern phones have rounded corners, Dynamic Islands/notches, and home indicators that obscure edge-to-edge elements if safe area insets are ignored.

codingChallenge.title: Implement a Mobile Screen Navigation Stack
codingChallenge.instructions: Write a JavaScript function `applyNavigation(initialStack, actions)` where `actions` is an array of `{ type: 'PUSH', screen: string }` or `{ type: 'POP' }`. POP should never remove the last remaining root screen. Return the resulting stack array.

visibleTests.description: Pushes two screens and pops the top screen

codingChallenge.solutionHint: Loop over `actions`: if `a.type === 'PUSH'` push `a.screen`; if `a.type === 'POP' && stack.length > 1` call `stack.pop()`.
